blocks.content: Imagine you have designed a banking system on paper classes like Account, Customer, Transaction. Everything looks clean and logical.
But then someone asks: "What does this actually look like at 3pm on a Tuesday when a real customer has two accounts and just made a transfer?"
That is the question an Object Diagram answers.
Where a class diagram shows the blueprint, an object diagram shows the building a frozen snapshot of real objects with real values at one specific moment in time.
1. What is an Object Diagram?
An Object Diagram is a UML diagram that captures the actual instances of classes and the links between them at a particular point during the system's execution.
It is not about what could exist. It is about what does exist right now.
Three things it tells you:
["Which objects are alive in the system at this moment","What values those objects are holding","How those objects are connected to each other"]
items: Which objects are alive in the system at this moment
What values those objects are holding
How those objects are connected to each other

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801647-d42efdb7.png
This is not a design. This is reality one specific customer, two specific accounts, concrete numbers filled in.
Components of an Object Diagram
Every object diagram is built from three building blocks.
1. Object

An object is a live instance of a class. Drawn as a rectangle with two sections. The top section carries the object name and class name in the format objectName : ClassName, always underlined. The bottom section lists the attribute values this specific instance is holding right now.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801750-a54b28d3.png
The underline is the key visual signal. It is what separates an object diagram from a class diagram at a glance.
Naming follows this pattern:
["john : Customer named instance, you know who this is",": Customer anonymous instance, the name does not matter here"]
items: john : Customer named instance, you know who this is
: Customer anonymous instance, the name does not matter here

blocks.content: 2. Attribute Values
Where a class diagram shows balance: double, an object diagram shows balance = 5000.00. Real data, not just types.
Every attribute carries an actual value. This is what makes object diagrams useful for debugging, testing scenarios, and illustrating how a design behaves with concrete data.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801995-9830815e.png
3. Links
A link is an instance of an association from the class diagram. Where a class diagram draws an arrow between two classes, an object diagram draws a link between two specific objects.
Links are drawn as solid lines, optionally labeled with the role name.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802132-db55e89e.png

blocks.content: Object Diagram vs Class Diagram
This is the comparison that trips most people up. They look similar but serve completely different purposes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802213-1a6f02bd.jpg
A class diagram says a Customer can own many Accounts. An object diagram shows that john owns savingsAcc and currentAccspecifically, with their exact balances at this moment.
When to Use an Object Diagram
blocks.text: When to Use an Object Diagram

blocks.content: Object diagrams do not replace class diagrams. They complement them. Reach for one when:

["Debugging a design your class diagram looks right but something feels off. Instantiate it with real values and the problem often becomes obvious.","Illustrating a scenario you want to show stakeholders exactly what a specific use case looks like with real data rather than abstract types.","Testing edge cases what does the system look like when a customer has zero accounts? Or ten? Object diagrams make these scenarios concrete.","Validating relationships does the multiplicity in your class diagram actually hold up with real instances? Draw it out and check."]
items: Debugging a design your class diagram looks right but something feels off. Instantiate it with real values and the problem often becomes obvious.
Illustrating a scenario you want to show stakeholders exactly what a specific use case looks like with real data rather than abstract types.
Testing edge cases what does the system look like when a customer has zero accounts? Or ten? Object diagrams make these scenarios concrete.
Validating relationships does the multiplicity in your class diagram actually hold up with real instances? Draw it out and check.

blocks.content: 2. Complete Example: Banking System Snapshot
Let's build a complete object diagram for a banking system at one specific moment in time.

The scenario: It is Tuesday afternoon. John Smith is a premium customer with a savings account and a current account. He just transferred £500 from his current account to his savings account. The transaction is recorded. His relationship manager is Sarah Jones.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245802335-2274e654.png
Reading the diagram

["john is a premium customer with two live accounts savings sitting at £8,500 and current at £6,500","txn1 captures the £500 transfer that just completed it links the current account that sent it and the savings account that received it","sarah is John's assigned relationship manager, based at the London Central branch","Every object is underlined, every attribute carries a real value, every link represents a real connection between real instances"]

blocks.content: This is the power of an object diagram. You are not looking at how the system could work. You are looking at exactly how it is working right now, at this moment, with these people and these numbers.
3. Object Diagram vs Class Diagram: A Library Walkthrough
blocks.text: 3. Object Diagram vs Class Diagram: A Library Walkthrough

blocks.content: Reading about the difference between a class diagram and an object diagram is one thing. Seeing the same small domain drawn twice, once as a blueprint and once as a snapshot of real instances, is what actually makes it click. Let us take a small library system and draw both, side by side.
The domain: Book and Member

The library system has two classes. A Book has a title, an ISBN, and a flag saying whether it is available. A Member has a name, a member ID, and a count of active loans. A book can be borrowed by a member, that single relationship ties the two classes together.
["Book attributes: title, isbn, available","Book behavior: checkOut, returnBook","Member attributes: name, memberId, activeLoans","Member behavior: borrow, returnItem"]
items: Book attributes: title, isbn, available
Book behavior: checkOut, returnBook
Member attributes: name, memberId, activeLoans
Member behavior: borrow, returnItem

blocks.content: The class diagram: the blueprint

The class diagram makes no claim about any particular book or person. It states the rule of the domain, a Book can be borrowed by a Member. No real title, no real name, just types and the shape of the relationship. This is true for every book and every member the library will ever have.
The object diagram: one Tuesday afternoon at the library
blocks.text: The object diagram: one Tuesday afternoon at the library

blocks.content: Now freeze the system at a real moment. It is Tuesday afternoon. A member named Priya Singh has just checked out a specific copy of Clean Code. That one fact, one book, one member, one active loan, is exactly what an object diagram captures.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783498469424-303199939.png
blocks.alt: Class diagram for Book and Member next to an object diagram snapshot showing one borrowed copy

blocks.content: Reading the contrast

["The class box named Book becomes the object box named b1 : Book, one specific copy sitting on a specific shelf","title: String becomes title = Clean Code, a real value takes the place of a type","The association labeled borrowedBy becomes a link between b1 and m1, a real connection between two real instances rather than a rule about all books and all members","Notice the object diagram drops the methods entirely, checkOut and borrow describe behavior the class supports, not state a snapshot needs to show"]
items: The class box named Book becomes the object box named b1 : Book, one specific copy sitting on a specific shelf
title: String becomes title = Clean Code, a real value takes the place of a type
The association labeled borrowedBy becomes a link between b1 and m1, a real connection between two real instances rather than a rule about all books and all members
Notice the object diagram drops the methods entirely, checkOut and borrow describe behavior the class supports, not state a snapshot needs to show

This side by side view is the fastest way to internalize the difference. Every element on the object diagram traces back to something on the class diagram, it has simply been filled in with a real instance and a real value.
4. Reading the Notation Correctly

Once you can tell a class diagram and an object diagram apart, the next skill is reading an object diagram accurately, knowing what each symbol is telling you, and knowing what has been left out on purpose.
What belongs on an object diagram
blocks.text: What belongs on an object diagram

blocks.content: ["The instance name and class name, always underlined, written as name : Class","Actual attribute values, using an equals sign rather than a colon, for example activeLoans = 1","Links between specific objects, drawn as plain solid lines","An optional role name on a link, added only when the relationship needs clarifying, for example borrowedBy"]
items: The instance name and class name, always underlined, written as name : Class
Actual attribute values, using an equals sign rather than a colon, for example activeLoans = 1
Links between specific objects, drawn as plain solid lines
An optional role name on a link, added only when the relationship needs clarifying, for example borrowedBy

blocks.content: What is deliberately left out
An object diagram is not a smaller class diagram. It leaves out entire categories of information on purpose, because those categories describe the class, not the moment being captured.

["Operations and methods, since a snapshot describes state, not behavior","Visibility modifiers like public or private, they describe the class contract, not a moment in time","Multiplicities on links, a link connects exactly one object to exactly one other object, there is nothing left to range over","Attributes that do not matter for the scenario being illustrated, you are free to omit anything irrelevant to the point you are making"]
items: Operations and methods, since a snapshot describes state, not behavior
Visibility modifiers like public or private, they describe the class contract, not a moment in time
Multiplicities on links, a link connects exactly one object to exactly one other object, there is nothing left to range over
Attributes that do not matter for the scenario being illustrated, you are free to omit anything irrelevant to the point you are making

blocks.title: A quick way to check yourself
blocks.text: If a value on your diagram could not be printed out and read by a person, for example checkOut or a visibility symbol, it probably does not belong on an object diagram.

blocks.content: Common mistakes

["Forgetting the underline under the instance name, without it a reader cannot tell an object from a class at a glance","Adding multiplicity labels to a link, multiplicities belong to associations between classes, not links between instances","Treating the diagram as a living document that must stay in sync forever, an object diagram is a snapshot, it is allowed to go stale the moment the scenario it describes changes","Drawing every attribute on every object regardless of relevance, cluttering the diagram defeats the purpose of illustrating one clear scenario"]
items: Forgetting the underline under the instance name, without it a reader cannot tell an object from a class at a glance
Adding multiplicity labels to a link, multiplicities belong to associations between classes, not links between instances
Treating the diagram as a living document that must stay in sync forever, an object diagram is a snapshot, it is allowed to go stale the moment the scenario it describes changes
Drawing every attribute on every object regardless of relevance, cluttering the diagram defeats the purpose of illustrating one clear scenario

blocks.content: Multiplicity lives on the class diagram, not here
blocks.text: Multiplicity lives on the class diagram, not here

blocks.content: Go back to the banking example from earlier. The class diagram says a Customer can own many Account instances, that rule is written once as a multiplicity like 1..*. The object diagram never repeats that rule. Instead it simply draws two separate links, one from john to savingsAcc and one from john to currentAcc. The multiplicity was the promise, the two links are the promise being kept in one particular case.

blocks.content: A one line way to tell them apart
blocks.text: A one line way to tell them apart

blocks.content: If a diagram has types and rules, it is a class diagram. If a diagram has real values and real names filled in, it is an object diagram. That single test settles almost every case you will run into.
How many objects should one diagram show
blocks.text: How many objects should one diagram show

blocks.content: There is no fixed rule, but the goal is always clarity about one specific scenario, not completeness about the whole system.

["Enough objects to make the scenario believable, a lone object with no links rarely explains anything","Few enough that a reader can trace every link with their eyes in a few seconds","If a scenario needs a dozen or more instances to make sense, that is usually a sign to split it into two smaller diagrams instead"]
items: Enough objects to make the scenario believable, a lone object with no links rarely explains anything
Few enough that a reader can trace every link with their eyes in a few seconds
If a scenario needs a dozen or more instances to make sense, that is usually a sign to split it into two smaller diagrams instead

blocks.content: Object diagrams next to sequence diagrams
blocks.text: Object diagrams next to sequence diagrams

blocks.content: Sequence diagrams borrow the exact same object notation, an instance name, a colon, a class name, underlined across the top of a lifeline. The difference is time. A sequence diagram follows that same object across a series of messages exchanged over time. An object diagram removes the time axis entirely and shows only one still frame, no messages, no ordering, just what exists and how it is connected right now.

{"pros":["Makes an abstract class diagram concrete and easy to sanity check","Excellent for walking a teammate or a stakeholder through one specific scenario with real data","Cheap to draw and genuinely disposable, there is no obligation to maintain it once the point has been made"],"cons":["Only ever describes one moment, it says nothing about how the system changes over time","Does not scale, a system with hundreds of live objects cannot be usefully drawn this way","Easy to let it drift out of date if it is mistaken for a permanent design artifact rather than a throwaway snapshot"]}
An object diagram is a photograph, not a blueprint. Use it to check that the blueprint actually produces the building you expected.

That is really the whole discipline. Draw the class diagram once to capture the rules of the domain. Draw an object diagram whenever you need to check those rules against a concrete, believable example, a real book, a real member, a real Tuesday afternoon.
5. Quick Recap
A short summary of everything above, useful as a refresher before an interview or a design review.

["A class diagram is the blueprint, it describes every possible instance of a class at once","An object diagram is a photograph, it describes specific instances with real attribute values at one moment","Instance names are always underlined, written as name : Class","Attribute values use an equals sign, never a colon, for example balance = 8500.00","Links replace associations, and links never carry multiplicity, each one connects exactly one object to exactly one other object","Operations, visibility modifiers, and multiplicities never appear on an object diagram, they belong to the class, not the snapshot"]
items: A class diagram is the blueprint, it describes every possible instance of a class at once
An object diagram is a photograph, it describes specific instances with real attribute values at one moment
Instance names are always underlined, written as name : Class
Attribute values use an equals sign, never a colon, for example balance = 8500.00
Links replace associations, and links never carry multiplicity, each one connects exactly one object to exactly one other object
Operations, visibility modifiers, and multiplicities never appear on an object diagram, they belong to the class, not the snapshot

blocks.title: Before you draw one
blocks.content: Do not reach for an object diagram to describe a trivial scenario a single sentence already explains. Save it for the moments where a confusing state, a tricky edge case, or a skeptical teammate needs to see concrete data before they will believe the design works.
Do object diagrams need to be kept up to date the way a class diagram does?

No. An object diagram documents one scenario at one point in time. Once that scenario has served its purpose, whether that is explaining a bug, walking through a use case, or checking a multiplicity, the diagram can be discarded without any loss. It was never meant to track the system going forward.
Can a single object diagram show more than one moment in time?

No, and this is a common point of confusion. An object diagram is a single still frame. If you need to show how objects and their links change across several steps, that is exactly what a sequence diagram or a communication diagram is for, both add a time or message dimension that an object diagram intentionally leaves out.
